2021_08_transmittal_letter_for_fy22_prop.paragraph: A transmittal letter dated April 5, 2021 from Oakland Schools Superintendent Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, forwarding the proposed FY 2021-22 Oakland Schools budget to constituent district boards of education for the review required by Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2). Oakland Schools projects a growth factor in its property tax revenues of 2.7% and cautions that a Headlee rollback of its operating millage is probable for FY 2021-22. Districts vote only on the General Fund budget, and each constituent board must adopt a resolution of support or non-support no later than June 1. The letter also reports that Oakland Schools' 2020-21 COVID-19 actions saved constituent districts approximately $1.9 million.
2021_08_transmittal_letter_for_fy22_prop.page:
**Origin**
Letter dated April 5, 2021 from Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent, Oakland Schools, addressed to "Board of Education Designate," with copies to the District Superintendent and District Business Manager. It accompanies the proposed FY 2021-22 Oakland Schools budget documents and appears in the Troy School District packet for the May 18, 2021 meeting.

**Statutory review process**
Per Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2021-22 General Fund budget is submitted to constituent district boards for review by May 1; not later than June 1 each constituent board must adopt a resolution of support or non-support. Oakland Schools supplies budgets for all of its funds for transparency, but LEA Designates vote only on the General Fund budget.

**Revenue outlook**
Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars. Projected growth factor in property tax revenues is 2.7%, described as conservative relative to Oakland County taxable value increase projections because a Headlee rollback of the operating millage is considered probable for FY 2021-22 (triggered when annual growth on existing property exceeds inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index). Additional information on taxable values and the millage reduction factor was expected by June 1.

**COVID-19 response**
2020-21 actions -- subsidies for Illuminate DnA and the Oakland Human Resource Consortium, elimination of ONE Network Fees, reduction in Shared Services IGA fees, carryover of CTE Regional Allocation funding, and payment of 100% of CTE transportation costs -- saved constituent districts approximately $1.9 million. Budgets cut in 2020-21 for travel, conference fees, printing and certain purchased services are reinstated in 2021-22. An estimated $2 million is provided in 2021-22 for tutoring, OSTC Supplemental Instruction, the Oakland Youth Innovation Lab and the Design Studio. Oakland Schools received no ESSER Fund, Governor's Emergency Education Relief Fund or MDE-distributed Coronavirus Relief Fund money and will not receive ESSER II; its COVID-19 expenditures are funded with tax revenues and state aid ISD funding.

**Programs and services**
The Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO) Project is a five-year, $5 million project launched in 2019-20. CTE receives additional resources including career program redesign and initial funding for a mobile classroom (the STEMi) beginning Spring 2020-21; the CTE allocation to LEAs was increased by more than 25% in 2019-20 and that level continues in 2021-22. Technology services are provided to fifteen constituent districts and business office services on a limited basis to four districts under intergovernmental agreements. MiPEER, formed in FY 2012-13 by Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County districts, is converting members to PowerSchool BusinessPlus in phases between 2015-16 and 2021-22. Illuminate Education has been the countywide assessment vendor since Fall 2016, covering 28 districts and two public school academies, with a 100% subsidy again in 2021-22. A countywide emergency radio communications channel is budgeted at $700,000 within a project estimated at $1.5 million.

**Personnel costs**
Step increases are included; no across-the-board salary increases are budgeted. The Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy retirement rate is projected to rise from 28.21% to 28.23% effective October 1, 2021, and Oakland Schools projects a blended rate of 28.23% for 2021-22. Health care hard cap limits, assuming 3.3% medical CPI growth:

| Tier | Plan year beginning after 1/1/21 | Plan year beginning after 1/1/22 (projected) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Family | $19,210.66 | $19,844.61 |
| Individual plus one | $14,730.96 | $15,217.08 |
| Single | $7,043.89 | $7,276.34 |

**PA-18 special education**
Property tax revenue growth of 2.7% is projected. The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local districts is budgeted to increase approximately $3.8 million or 2.8%, with $3.9 million budgeted for other LEA distributions. In FY 2020-21 Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $5.6 million above the base distribution.

**Calendar**
Presentation to 28 local district business managers at the Oakland County School Business Officials meeting on April 23, 2021; Designates Meeting April 27 at 6:00 PM; district resolutions due on or before June 1, 2021; Truth in Budgeting hearing and board consideration of the FY 2021-22 budget documents on June 1. Questions to 248.209.2424.
2021_08_transmittal_letter_for_fy22_prop.verbose:
**Document and authorship.** Transmittal letter dated April 5, 2021, signed by Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent of Oakland Schools, addressed to "Dear Board of Education Designate," with a copy line to the District Superintendent and the District Business Manager. It introduces the enclosed proposed Oakland Schools budget for FY 2021-22 and appears in the Troy School District board materials for the meeting of May 18, 2021.

**Statutory submission and voting.** Per the Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2021-22 General Fund budget is to be submitted to each constituent district's Board of Education for review by May 1. Not later than June 1, the board of each constituent district shall adopt a resolution of support or non-support of the General Fund budget. For transparency purposes Oakland Schools includes the budgets for all of its funds in the enclosed document; however, it is only the General Fund budget upon which constituent districts vote, and the letter twice stresses that LEA Designates vote only on the General Fund budget.

**Property tax revenue and Headlee.** Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars. The letter projects a growth factor in Oakland Schools' property tax revenues of 2.7%. Tax revenue projections are described as conservative compared to Oakland County taxable value increase projections because there is concern that a Headlee rollback of the operating millage is probable for FY 2021-22. A rollback occurs when the annual growth on existing property is greater than the rate of inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Additional information on taxable values and the millage reduction factor was to be received by June 1.

**COVID-19 response.** The 2020-21 COVID-19 response included subsidies for Illuminate DnA and the Oakland Human Resource Consortium, elimination of ONE Network Fees, reduction in Shared Services IGA fees, carryover of CTE Regional Allocation funding, and payment of 100% of CTE transportation costs. These actions on behalf of the Oakland Schools Board of Education saved constituent districts approximately $1.9 million in 2020-21. Oakland Schools significantly reduced 2020-21 budgets for travel, conference fees, printing and certain other purchased services; those budgets are reinstated in 2021-22 as operations are expected to slowly return to pre-pandemic status, subject to monitoring and the amendment process. Resources developed for districts include guidance to evaluate, measure and assess well-being within school communities; best practices for remote and hybrid teaching and learning; and curriculum, instruction, and assessment toolkits. Oakland Schools is providing an estimated $2 million in 2021-22 for additional learning opportunities for students and professional learning for teachers, including Tutoring, OSTC Supplemental Instruction, the Oakland Youth Innovation Lab, and the Design Studio. Financial support to local districts in 2021-22 includes a full subsidy of Illuminate DnA base costs and allowing districts to carry over the unspent portion of their CTE Regional Allocation from 2020-21 to 2021-22. Unlike local districts, Oakland Schools has not received funding under the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief Fund (ESSER Fund), the Governor's Emergency Education Relief Fund, or the Coronavirus Relief Fund distributed by MDE, and will not receive funding under ESSER II; its COVID-19 related expenditures are funded with tax revenues and state aid ISD funding.

**Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO).** The LEO Project is centered on ensuring early literacy success for children in Oakland County. It is a five-year, $5 million project launched during the 2019-20 school year, developed to be deeply rooted in research, to build capacity in districts, to be tailored to the needs of districts, and to focus on job-embedded professional learning.

**Career and Technical Education.** To align with the Michigan Department of Education's Top 10 in 10 Years goals and strategies, additional resources are dedicated to career and technical education. Beyond significant resources for the four technical campuses, the 2021-22 budget adds funds for career program redesign and initial funding for a CTE mobile classroom (the STEMi) intended to bring STEM activities to local districts beginning in Spring 2020-21. In 2019-20 the CTE allocation to LEAs was increased by more than 25%, and that level of funding continues in 2021-22, providing local districts additional resources for local CTE programs from elementary to high school.

**Shared Services.** Oakland Schools provides technology, business office, instruction, and truancy services on a cost recovery basis. Technology services are currently provided to fifteen constituent districts, and business office services are provided on a limited basis to four districts through an intergovernmental agreement (IGA).

**MiPEER Consortium.** In FY 2012-13, Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts formed the Michigan Partnership for Essential Education Resources (MIPEER) to select a countywide Enterprise Resource Planning system for human resource and financial applications. The consortium standardized the Chart of Accounts and created best practice business processes for finance, human resources, budgeting and procurement. Members are converting to the PowerSchool BusinessPlus software in phases between 2015-16 and 2021-22.

**Illuminate.** Oakland Schools has contracted with Illuminate Education as its countywide student assessment and data analysis tool vendor since the Fall of 2016; all twenty-eight (28) districts and two (2) public school academies are included in the software license and support agreement. Illuminate DnA lets teachers build and administer formative assessments, capture and analyze multiple sources of data, and direct students to learning resources for targeted standards. The Oakland Schools Board of Education agreed to provide a 100% subsidy for the student assessment software and support again in 2021-22; add-ons called "Item Banks" may be purchased through the contract at the districts' cost.

**Subsidies.** Beyond Illuminate DnA, Oakland Schools provides multiple software products at no cost or reduced cost in career and technical education and in curriculum and assessment; a subsidy on the per pupil cost of the PowerSchool BusinessPlus system for MiPEER consortium members; and communication tools such as news services and media monitoring/clipping services at no cost to LEAs. These are exclusive of pass-through grant funds, other district allocations, and the cost of dedicated staff who support student and finance/HR software and applications.

**Countywide Communications Channel.** The 2021-22 General Education Fund budget includes $700,000 for a countywide communications channel, a multi-year project intended to connect constituent districts to first responders via an emergency radio channel. The total cost of the project is estimated at $1.5 million.

**Personnel costs.** Step increases for eligible employees are included in the 2021-22 budget, but no across-the-board salary increases are included due to funding uncertainties at publication. Decisions on salary increases will follow the May Revenue Estimating Conference, final taxable value reports from Oakland County Equalization (generally received in May), and more concrete State budget information; all union salary changes including step adjustments are subject to collective bargaining. On the State-mandated retirement rate, there are 8 rates in effect depending on hire date and retirement benefit choices; the most common choice, Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy, is projected to increase from 28.21% to 28.23% beginning October 1, 2021, and Oakland Schools projects an overall blended retirement rate of 28.23% for 2021-22. The "Hard Cap" for employee health care costs remains in effect for all labor groups; limits are adjusted annually based on the medical price index, and Oakland Schools projects growth in the medical price index of 3.3%. Under that assumption the limits move from $19,210.66 to $19,844.61 for Family, from $14,730.96 to $15,217.08 for Individual plus one, and from $7,043.89 to $7,276.34 for Single, comparing plan years beginning after 1/1/21 with projected plan years beginning after 1/1/22.

**PA-18 Special Education Funding.** Oakland Schools receives property tax revenue for support of Special Education programs, with growth in property tax revenue projected at 2.7% for FY 2021-22. The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $3.8 million or 2.8%. Additionally, $3.9 million is budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group home expenditures, reimbursements to districts for educating incarcerated youth, special education program startup, extraordinary expenditures, and capital. In FY 2020-21, Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $5.6 million above the base distribution.

**Planning for the future.** Oakland Schools uses a five-year forecast updated with each budget amendment that incorporates Oakland County Equalization taxable value projections, and maintains a five-year capital plan updated annually. The organization pre-funds at least three years and up to five years of the capital plan requirements.

**Schedule.** A presentation of the budget to the 28 local school district business managers was scheduled for the Oakland County School Business Officials meeting on April 23, 2021. The Oakland Schools Board of Education planned a Designates Meeting on April 27 at 6:00 PM so local board designates and district administration could review the General Fund budget before submitting board resolutions to Oakland Schools on or before June 1, 2021. The Oakland Schools Board of Education would hold a Truth in Budgeting hearing on June 1 and consider the FY 2021-22 proposed budget documents for approval during its regular meeting that night. Questions are directed to 248.209.2424.

2021_12_mhsaa_2021_22handbooksupplement.paragraph: The Michigan High School Athletic Association's 2021-22 Handbook Supplement, included in the Troy School District board packet for July 20, 2021, listing substantive regulation changes in place of a printed handbook. The full 2021-22 Handbook (red cover) is available only online to school administrators at MHSAA.com, and the supplement is to be inserted into the 2020-21 Handbook (royal blue cover). Among the changes, the COVID-era adjustments page is declared obsolete, the minimum Previous Academic Credit Record of 66% is again waived for fall 2021-22 sports, and any student born before Sept. 1, 2002 is ineligible for interscholastic scrimmages or contests.
2021_12_mhsaa_2021_22handbooksupplement.page:
**Purpose and distribution**
Because of the COVID-19 pandemic and a small number of regulation changes, the 2021-22 MHSAA Handbook was not printed. The full 2021-22 Handbook (red cover) is available to school administrators logged in at MHSAA.com under School Administrator Services. The supplement contains substantive changes only, is posted online, and is to be inserted into the 2020-21 Handbook (royal blue cover); changes are gray shaded. Copies are designated for the AD and the Principal. MHSAA 2021-22 Membership Resolutions were mailed to superintendents via US Mail on May 11, 2021 and are due back to the MHSAA by Aug. 1, 2021.

**Eligibility changes**
Page 25, the COVID-19 pandemic adjustments page, is obsolete and all references to it are to be disregarded. The MHSAA minimum Previous Academic Credit Record (66%) is again waived for sports played in the fall of 2021-22; the Pre-Participation physical exam returns for 2021-22 and the Health Questionnaire is not in use. Page 31, Regulation I, Section 2(A): a participant must be under nineteen (19) years of age, except that a student whose nineteenth birthday occurs on or after September 1 of a current school year is eligible for the balance of that year; any student born before Sept. 1, 2002 is ineligible. Page 33, Regulation I, Section 4, Interpretation 24 and Interpretation 46 govern students splitting classwork between 8th and 9th grades, with thresholds of 3 of 4, 4 of 5 or 6, 5 of 7, and 6 of 8 high school classes; the 66% allowance applies only to a student in the 8th grade for the first time. Page 47, Regulation I, Section 9, Interpretation 77-b tightens proof of a full residential change. Page 56, Regulation I, Section 12(C) permits a student who has completed a 12th-grade season to play in one high school all-star event held after the MHSAA Final in that sport, with written notice to the MHSAA at least 30 calendar days prior.

**Cooperative programs, coaches and officials**
Page 29, Regulation I, Section 1(E-2) makes permanent the allowance for cooperative agreements in nine sports between public schools of the same district: baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis and wrestling. Page 61, Regulation II, Section 3(B) requires CPR certification attestation for varsity head coaches, extending to JV and 9th-grade head coaches effective Aug. 1, 2022. Page 64, Regulation II, Section 7(A) requires that only MHSAA registered officials who have completed a current year's rules meeting may officiate high school regular season or tournament contests; a rules meeting is not required for middle school contests.

**Competition limits and dates**
Page 67, Regulation II, Section 10(A): in basketball a student may play no more than five quarters in a day, no more than three days of competition in a week Monday through Sunday, and no more than 20 days of competition exclusive of the MHSAA tournament; a team is limited to three games Monday through Sunday, four interscholastic scrimmages and 20 games, and one game per day; overtime counts as an extension of the 4th quarter. Pages 71 and 72 set fall practice at Aug. 9, 2021, spring practice at March 14, 2022, and winter practice dates from Nov. 1 through Nov. 22, 2021 by sport. Any student born before Sept. 1, 2002 is ineligible for interscholastic scrimmages or contests at an MHSAA member school in an MHSAA tournament sport. Regulation III, Section 2(D) governs Eligibility Advancement.

**Page 33 -- Regulation I, Section 4, maximum enrollment.** Interpretation 24: a student whose classwork is divided between the 8th and 9th grades is considered enrolled in the grade carrying the major part of the work, and in the 8th grade if the amounts are equal. **Instrument**
MHSAA Membership Resolution for the year August 1, 2021 through July 31, 2022, addressed from the Michigan High School Athletic Association, 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, (517) 332-5046. The MHSAA is described as a voluntary, nonprofit corporation of public, private and parochial junior high/middle and senior high schools whose boards of education or governing bodies have applied for and received membership. Resolutions that are modified in any way, or supplemented with letters placing additional conditions on membership or tournament participation, are rejected; one signed copy is returned to the MHSAA and one retained.

**Adopting body**
Troy Board of Education, City/Township of Troy, County of Oakland, State of Michigan. Record of adoption shows the resolution adopted on the 20th day of July, 2021 for the Troy schools. Address given as 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, with contact e-mail jholmes@troy.k12.mi.us. Signature lines are provided for the Board Secretary or designee.

**Effect of adoption**
The listed schools are enrolled as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc. and are further enrolled to participate in the approved interschool athletic activities it sponsors. The board delegates to the Superintendent or designee the responsibility for supervision and control of those activities, accepts the association's Constitution and By-Laws, and adopts as its own the rules, regulations and interpretations published in the current Handbook as minimum standards, agreeing to primary enforcement. Schools that host or participate in association meets and tournaments must follow and enforce all tournament policies, procedures and schedules. Tournaments are the collective property of the MHSAA, not of any individual member school. The authorization is effective from August 1, 2021 until July 31, 2022 and may not be revoked during that period.

**Membership eligibility rules**
A school building must have enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students, whether for grades 6 through 8 or 9, grades 7 through 8 or 9, or grades 9 or 10 through 12; a nonpublic school must qualify for federal income tax exemption as a not-for-profit organization. Schools may join at the 6th-grade level to reach the 15-student minimum whether or not 6th-graders participate in athletics. Districts are not required to join at the junior high/middle school level or to sponsor athletics for 6th-grade students, but if a listed middle school sponsors a 6th-grade team or lets a 6th-grader play with 7th and 8th graders, all of Regulations III and IV apply to all 6th-graders in all such sports.

**Schools listed for 2021-22**
High schools: Athens High School and Troy High School. Junior high/middle schools: Larson Middle School, Baker Middle School, Boulan Park Middle School and Smith Middle School. Grade configuration is entered as 6-8. Anticipated 2021-22 enrollment figures entered on the first sheet are 431, 197, 530, 251, 467 and 238; on the continuation sheet Smith Middle School shows 372 and 200.

2021_14_8_17_21_boe_strategic_planning_r.paragraph: A PowerPoint presentation titled "Strategic Planning 2026 Recommendations: Update on Stakeholder Planning," delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on August 17, 2021. It reviews the district's five-year strategic plan redesign process -- See, Engage, Act -- reports stakeholder feedback from collaborative teams, and presents refreshed statements for the Green, Red, Blue and Gold pillars. 2021_14_8_17_21_boe_strategic_planning_r.page:
**Presentation**
Strategic Planning 2026 Recommendations: Update on Stakeholder Planning, August 17, 2021, to the Troy School District Board of Education. Outline: overview of the strategic planning process, current state, future state, and a preview of the accountability plan. The redesign process is framed as See, Engage, Act, aimed at system coherence in a 5-Year Strategic Plan in which research defines world class.

**Stakeholder feedback**
Key wonderings from collaborative teams: accountability is missing, specifically data and collective commitments; continue with clarity and simple understanding of a complex process; coordination and how the pillars interact; define deep learning; Red Pillar understanding; equity and inclusion not specifically called out; the Gold Pillar should include ALL staff, students and families; and the Green Pillar should include a through line to career with a focus on access and exposure to career.

**Research base**
Fullan 2021 is cited for the right drivers for system success: Well-being and Learning, Social Intelligence, Equality Investments, and Systemness. Louis et al., 2010 and the Wallace Foundation study of effective district leadership are cited for the point that district leaders must be crystal clear and repetitive in communicating the agenda for action, but that the best indicator of coherence is when system members experience it -- the ability to "talk the walk." A further quotation notes that most strategic plans are high on aspirations and almost empty on HOW to achieve the goals.

**Pillar refreshes**
Green Pillar, Investing in Early Childhood to Career: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education including advocating for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, broaden access to computer science and CTE, connect underrepresented students to in-demand high-growth sectors, and build partnerships supporting work-based learning, credentials and college credit. Red Pillar, Ensuring a Focus on Equity and Well-Being: safely reopen schools and support students disproportionately impacted by the pandemic; fund whole-child supports including community schools with wraparound services such as afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; assess and act on facility upgrade needs. Blue Pillar, Deepening Learning for All: create and sustain systems of support that deepen learning and empower student voice; improve technology access for students and families with quality training; pursue global best practices in all content areas. Gold Pillar, Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families: improve educator preparation, strengthen pipelines for underrepresented educators, sustain job-embedded professional learning, and co-design impactful learning experiences for staff, community and students.

**Resource allocation and next steps**
Increased social workers and counseling in all buildings; Red Pillar professional learning on Tuesday, August 24 with Dr. Jean Clinton; Media 2.0 positions; sustained literacy coaching and interventions; expanded job-embedded coaching for literacy and math; ELD support; coordinated instructional support; a Delayed Start Model providing 90 minutes for collaboration through professional learning; and Accountability Plan co-design with a report to the Board in the second semester. Other items include summer professional learning dates, new teacher orientation, an Apple technology refresh in ALL elementary buildings, and shared leadership of pillar teams.

**Accountability plan preview**
System-level implementation considerations: build cohesive leadership teams with systemness including all departments; create clarity by focusing on a FEW things; overcommunicate clarity; identify objectives and key results; establish timelines. A cabinet example sets the objective of sustaining a world class school system with key results of visiting five classrooms per week, aligning vision with facility enhancement through six collaborative meetings with a community team, hosting six meetings for all support staff in CO and Services, and improving internal communication with Cabinet notes twice per month. The closing section commits the leadership team to the OneTroy values of cultivating a collaborative culture, deepening learning, and focusing direction, with the vision of world class for ALL.
2021_14_8_17_21_boe_strategic_planning_r.verbose:
**Presentation identity.** "Strategic Planning 2026 Recommendations: Update on Stakeholder Planning," a PowerPoint delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on August 17, 2021. The presentation outline covers an overview of the strategic planning process, current state, future state, and a preview of the accountability plan.

**Current state and process.** The current-state section is titled Building on Success. The redesign process is described as See, Engage, Act. System coherence is pursued through a 5-Year Strategic Plan with a VISION (WHAT) element and the premise that research defines world class. A slide on clarifying the foundation is followed by guiding questions posed to stakeholders: for current state, what are we proud of and what are we challenged by; for future state, what is possible over the next five years.

**Stakeholder feedback -- key wonderings from collaborative teams.** Accountability is missing, specifically data and collective commitments. Continue with clarity and simple understanding of a complex process. Coordination and how the pillars interact. Define deep learning. Red Pillar understanding. Equity and Inclusion are not specifically called out. The Gold Pillar should include ALL staff, students and families. The Green Pillar should include a through line to career with a focus on access and exposure to career.

**Research cited.** Under "Latest Research on Key Drivers, Fullan 2021," the right drivers for system success are listed as Well-being and Learning, Social Intelligence, Equality Investments, and Systemness. A slide titled Challenge -- Coherence and Clarity quotes Louis et al., 2010, that district leaders must "be crystal clear and repetitive when communicating the district's agenda for action," then argues that the true test of coherence is not a leader's ability to explain alignment but whether system members experience it, described as the ability of individuals and the group to "talk the walk" -- embedded coherence. Whole-system reform is characterized as coherence making: when systems focus on structural elements such as having meetings and stipulating agendas they end up being just another program, because the reform comes from the mindsets behind them. The slide urges an asset lens that recognizes strengths in people and invests belief in them.

**Future state framing.** A slide asks What's Next, quoting that the world's best school systems ensure all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities and goals of the system, with leaders clarifying a few very specific non-negotiables that must be honored throughout the system while encouraging autonomy and creativity at all levels to foster ownership and innovation.

**Green Pillar Refresh -- Investing in Early Childhood to Career.** Continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool for all three and four-year-olds and access for all. Expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, aiming to provide more students with access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science, connect underrepresented students to careers in in-demand, high-growth industry sectors, and include partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers and other stakeholders that allow students to engage in quality work-based learning opportunities, earn a credential, and/or earn college credit.

**Red Pillar Refresh -- Ensuring a Focus on Equity and Well-Being.** Safely reopen schools and support students, particularly those disproportionately impacted by the pandemic. Fund additional investments to support the needs of the whole child, including community schools that provide wraparound services such as afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists. Assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

**Blue Pillar Refresh -- Deepening Learning for All.** Create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice, with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children. Improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage use of technology to deepen learning. Continue to pursue the global best practices of all content areas.

**Gold Pillar Refresh -- Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families.** Improve educator preparation, strengthen pipelines for underrepresented educators, and support current educators. Continue to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff. Provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.

**Resource allocation and simple next steps.** Increased social workers and counseling in all buildings. Emphasis on Red Pillar professional learning on Tuesday, August 24, with Dr. Jean Clinton. Media 2.0 positions. Sustained support for literacy coaching and literacy interventions. Expanded job-embedded coaching for literacy and math. ELD support. Coordinated instructional support. A Delayed Start Model to ensure collaboration through professional learning, at 90 minutes. Accountability Plan co-design, with a report out to the Board of Education in the second semester. Other dates and opportunities listed are summer professional learning dates, new teacher orientation, an Apple technology refresh in ALL elementary buildings, and shared leadership of pillar teams.

**Accountability plan preview -- distributing leadership.** The presentation cites the landmark study of effective district leadership supported by the Wallace Foundation, which concluded that district leaders must "be crystal clear and repetitive when communicating the district's agenda for action," and repeats that the best indicator of coherence is when system members experience it. It states that most strategic plans are high on aspirations and almost empty on HOW to achieve the goals, and that when virtually all members of a group articulate the same story in terms of goals, strategies and progress -- knowing what they are doing and WHY -- it is a powerful indicator of widespread ownership and cultural coherence, making improvement efforts far more likely to be sustainable.

**Next steps for system-level implementation.** Key considerations are to build cohesive leadership teams with systemness including all departments; create clarity by focusing on a FEW things; overcommunicate clarity; identify objectives and key results; and establish timelines. The implementation plan slide is headed Meaningful Teams and returns to the Foundation. A Blueprint Preview states that teams will report out to the Board of Education in the second semester, that Project 2026 is in draft, and that objectives and key results will be continually monitored. The Project 2026 Blueprint is organized at District, School and Troy levels.

**Measuring what matters -- cabinet example.** Objective: sustaining a world class school system. Key results: visit five classrooms per week; align vision with facility enhancement through six collaborative meetings with a community team; host six meetings for all support staff in CO and Services; and improve internal communication with Cabinet notes twice per month. A subsequent section outlines the Green Pillar in terms of Overview, Objectives and Key Results.

**Closing accountability statement.** Continuing the world class journey to 2026 is described as the largest and most important challenge the district has undertaken, large in terms of commitment. The leadership team re-commits to carrying out the mission of ensuring learning for ALL, with the vision of world class for ALL described as ambitious and as a challenge to hold the team accountable to newly established goals co-designed with the teams in place. As OneTroy, the district will carry out its values of cultivating a collaborative culture, deepening learning, and focusing direction, with the success of the plan expected to highlight a significant impact on students, and staff told they will play a major role in ensuring a world class learning environment for ALL.
